extraction.name: SeamlessM4T
extraction.description: SeamlessM4T is a massively multilingual and multimodal machine translation system that supports speech-to-speech translation, speech-to-text translation, text-to-speech translation, text-to-text translation, and automatic speech recognition. The work introduces SeamlessAlign, a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations of more than 470,000 hours, and reports using a filtered subset combined with human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data totaling 406,000 hours to train the model.
extraction.creator: Meta AI

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The paper describes creating SeamlessAlign, a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations totaling more than 470,000 hours. Starting with 4 million hours of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, the authors chunked files into overlapping segments, applied speech language identification, and mined alignments against sentence-segmented text drawn from NLLB. Speech and text corpora were projected into a common embedding space and mined to identify translation pairs with optimal segmentation. The final training data for SeamlessM4T combined a filtered subset of SeamlessAlign with human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data totaling 406,000 hours.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For CVSS evaluation, the paper notes that some samples from the evaluation data were missing in 8 out of 21 languages: Catalan, German, Estonian, French, Italian, Mongolian, Persian, and Portuguese.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw audio started from 4 million hours originating from a publicly available repository of crawled web data. On the text side, the work relied entirely on the same sentence-segmented dataset deployed in NLLB. Additional human-labeled resources mentioned include parallel text collections and speech collections such as CoVoST and mTEDx, and the model training also used human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors deduplicated audio file URLs, downloaded audio files, resampled them at 16KHz, filtered non-speech data with a bespoke audio event detection model, segmented audio with voice activity detection, applied speech language identification, created overlapping over-segmented splits, projected speech and text into a shared SONAR embedding space, and mined alignments using FAISS and a margin criterion. For model training, they selected top-ranked mined pairs up to specified hour caps per direction based on SONAR alignment scores.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text preprocessing reused the same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps as NLLB and ran them at scale with Stopes. For audio preprocessing, the authors deduplicated URLs, downloaded files, resampled at 16KHz, filtered non-speech with an audio event detection model, segmented with an open voice activity detection model, applied speech language identification, and created overlapping splits. For human-labeled data, they removed special tokens such as <silence> and <no-speech>, filtered examples exceeding 100 sub-word tokens, and removed pairs with skewed text-to-audio length ratio above 5 sub-words per second. Additional filtering removed pairs with toxicity imbalance above 1, utterances shorter than 0.1 seconds or longer than 50 seconds, texts longer than 250 sub-words, and texts containing more than 20% emojis, more than 50% punctuations, or more than 50% spaces.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The paper describes several annotation processes. Human-labeled and pseudo-labeled data were used in training. ASR data were pseudo-labeled with the multilingual T2TT model NLLB-200-3.3B to create additional S2TT supervision. For human evaluation, S2TT and S2ST outputs were annotated with the XSTS protocol for semantic similarity, and S2ST outputs were also annotated with MOS for naturalness, sound quality, and clarity. In XSTS, 3 annotators examined each source-target pair; if the 3 annotators disagreed by 2 or more score values, 2 additional annotators evaluated the item, and the median score was taken. Calibration items were intermixed and language-level scores were calibrated using a cross-lingual calibration set. For MOS, 3 annotators scored each generation for most languages, while some languages received scores from a single annotator per item, and the median score was collected.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For XSTS and MOS, the paper reports using the median score over annotators for robustness. In XSTS, items with disagreement of 2 or more among the initial 3 annotators were re-evaluated by 2 additional annotators, bringing the total to 5 for those items. Language-level XSTS scores were calibrated using a cross-lingual calibration set and moderated calibration methodology to reduce annotator bias. The paper also discusses limitations such as annotator bias, recency bias, and the small number of annotators per item.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 annotators per item for XSTS, with 2 additional annotators when the initial 3 disagreed by 2 or more; 3 annotators per item for most MOS evaluations, with some languages receiving 1 annotator per item
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The paper states that up to 30 annotators were used per language pair for XSTS, each item was shown to 3 annotators assigned essentially randomly, and all annotators went through monolingual English practice evaluations. No further annotator demographic details are provided.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: NLLB-200-3.3B for pseudo-labeling ASR data; in-house ASR model for generating text transcriptions for mined S2ST data; Whisper-Large-v2 and Whisper-Medium for ASR-based evaluation and transcription in ASR-BLEU, ASR-chrF, and ASR-ETOX; ETOX for toxicity detection
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper states that all contributions, including models, inference code, finetuning recipes backed by Fairseq2, and metadata to recreate the unfiltered 470,000 hours of SeamlessAlign, are open-sourced and accessible at the GitHub repository. It also states that the current version of mining focused on 37 target languages and scaling to all 100 languages will be explored in future iterations. No explicit maintenance schedule or deprecation policy is provided.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The paper discusses and evaluates gender bias and added toxicity. It also references demographic axes in HolisticBias and Multilingual HolisticBias including ability, age, body type, characteristics, cultural background, gender and sex, nationality, political ideologies, race/ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, and socioeconomic class. It further discusses speaker variations and user demographics such as gender, race, accent, and language.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that SeamlessM4T could augment world-readiness by streamlining multilingual exchange across contexts, improving accessibility for people who lack reading or writing skills and for people who are blind or visually impaired, and helping languages with multiple writing systems. It also notes potential risks: groups with lower levels of digital literacy may become more vulnerable to misinformation or online scams, personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated from mined web data, and toxic, biased, or false outputs could adversely impact users, especially in health and safety contexts. The authors state that SeamlessM4T-fueled applications should be viewed as augmentation devices rather than replacements for language learning or reliable human interpreters, especially in legal or medical decision-making.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper evaluates gender bias and reports that SeamlessM4T overgeneralizes to masculine forms when translating from neutral terms, with an average preference of about 10%, and shows a lack of robustness when varying gender by about 3%. It also reports overrepresentation of masculine lexica compared to feminine in analyzed datasets. The paper notes that ASR performance may vary based on gender, race, accent, or language, and that translation quality and toxicity vary by language and demographic axis.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper states that SeamlessM4T is a research model and is not released for production deployment. It is trained on general-domain data and is not intended for domain-specific inputs such as medical or legal domains, is not intended for long-form translation, and translations cannot be used as certified translations. Additional limitations discussed include noisy or missing evaluation samples, limited speaker diversity in Fleurs-based human evaluation, limited annotator sample sizes, possible truncation and omission in S2ST outputs, and limitations of word-list-based toxicity and gender detection methods, including context sensitivity, tokenization issues, and ASR-induced false negatives.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The paper states that SeamlessM4T is primarily intended for research in speech and text translation. Supported uses include ASR for 96 languages, S2ST from 100 source speech languages into 35 target speech languages, S2TT from 100 source speech languages into 95 target text languages, T2ST from 95 source text languages into 35 target speech languages, T2TT from 95 source text languages into 95 target text languages, and TTS for 36 languages. The released artifacts include model weights, inference code, fine-tuning recipes, tools for creating aligned speech data, metadata to recreate SeamlessAlign, Stopes-based pipelines, SONAR encoders, and Blaser 2.0.
